content: Fear of pain during the insertion of intrauterine contraception (IUC) is a significant barrier to its use. IUC includes copper-containing intrauterine devices and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems. Various interventions have been studied to manage pain during IUC insertion, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), local cervical anesthetics, and cervical ripening agents like misoprostol. A systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions in reducing pain associated with IUC insertion. The primary outcomes assessed were self-reported pain at the time of tenaculum placement, during IUC insertion, and up to six hours post-insertion. The review included 33 trials with a total of 5,710 participants, most of which were conducted between 2010 and 2015. The interventions studied included lidocaine, misoprostol, NSAIDs, and other agents. The findings are as follows: 1. Lidocaine: Topical 2% lidocaine gel showed no significant effect on pain during tenaculum placement or IUC insertion in meta-analyses of two and three trials, respectively. Other lidocaine formulations demonstrated efficacy in individual trials. For example, lidocaine and prilocaine cream reduced IUC insertion pain (mean difference [MD] -1.96, 95% confidence interval [CI] -3.00 to -0.92). Among nulliparous women, a 4% lidocaine formulation significantly reduced pain scores within 10 minutes (MD -15.90, 95% CI -22.77 to -9.03) and at 30 minutes post-insertion (MD -11.10, 95% CI -19.05 to -3.15). In parous women, a 10% lidocaine spray reduced IUC insertion pain (median pain score 1.00 versus 3.00). A 1% lidocaine paracervical block reduced pain at tenaculum placement compared to no intervention (median pain score 12 versus 28). 2. Misoprostol: Meta-analysis showed that misoprostol was associated with higher pain scores during IUC insertion compared to placebo (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.27, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.46). Cramping was more likely with misoprostol use (odds ratio [OR] 2.64, 95% CI 1.46 to 4.76). In nulliparous women, misoprostol was associated with higher pain scores during insertion (median 46 versus 34) and before leaving the clinic (MD 7.60, 95% CI 6.48 to 8.72; medians 35.5 versus 20.5). However, in one trial, nulliparous women using misoprostol were less likely to experience moderate or severe pain during insertion (OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.55) and were more likely to rate the experience favorably. Misoprostol combined with diclofenac was associated with side effects such as shivering, headache, and abdominal pain. Participants in these trials had no history of vaginal delivery. In one trial, women in the misoprostol group were less likely to choose or recommend the treatment in the future. 3. NSAIDs: Among multiparous women, tramadol 50 mg was more effective than naproxen 550 mg in reducing IUC insertion pain (MD -0.63, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.32). Naproxen was more effective than placebo in reducing pain (MD -1.94, 95% CI -2.35 to -1.53). Women in the naproxen group were less likely to report the insertion experience as unpleasant and were more likely to want the medication in the future. An older trial showed that repeated doses of naproxen 300 mg reduced pain scores at one hour (MD -1.04, 95% CI -1.67 to -0.41) and two hours (MD -0.98, 95% CI -1.64 to -0.32) post-insertion. Most participants in this trial were nulliparous and also received a lidocaine paracervical block. In conclusion, most of the evidence regarding the effectiveness of these interventions is of moderate quality and often derived from single trials. Lidocaine 2% gel, misoprostol, and most NSAIDs were not effective in reducing pain during IUC insertion. However, certain lidocaine formulations, tramadol, and naproxen showed some efficacy in specific populations. Interventions that were found to be ineffective do not warrant further research.
